records.sourceFile: How does sleep help recovery from exercise-induced muscle injuries.pdf

paper.citation: Chennaoui M, Vanneau T, Trignol A, Arnal P, Gomez-Merino D, Baudot C, et al. How does sleep help recovery from exercise-induced muscle injuries? J Sci Med Sport. 2021.
paper.abstract: This narrative review describes how sleep and the circadian system regulate hormonal and immune responses, and how sleep relates to injury risk in athletes and soldiers. It then reviews the phases of muscle regeneration and the effects of sleep deprivation and sleep extension on muscle tissue. The authors propose that sleep extension could aid recovery from exercise-induced muscle injury through higher local IGF-I and better control of local inflammation.
paper.tldr: Sleep loss shifts hormones and inflammation in ways that could slow muscle repair after injury. Sleep extension is a plausible recovery strategy, but the authors state that human evidence on sleep and muscle injury recovery is lacking.
paper.methods: Narrative review. No systematic search method is described. The authors summarise sleep physiology, sleep in athletes and military personnel, muscle regeneration, and the effects of sleep deprivation and sleep extension on muscle repair.
paper.findings: Acute and chronic sleep loss raise catabolic hormones and markers of systemic inflammation, and in a rodent model it impaired muscle regeneration after injury. In humans, extending sleep by under 1 hour a day for seven days increased circulating IGF-1 in healthy young men. The authors state that there is no data in healthy humans on sleep interventions and inflammation after muscle injury.
paper.limitations: The review is narrative and does not describe a systematic search, so the sources selected cannot be checked. Most of the muscle-repair evidence comes from rodent models, and the human sleep-extension data come from healthy young men without muscle injury. The authors call for direct studies before clear guidelines are possible.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can explain to athletes that poor sleep may slow recovery and raise injury risk, and promote sleep hygiene, such as limiting bright light and noise and controlling bedroom temperature. Sleep extension may be worth considering as part of recovery, but the review does not give dosing or timing for injured athletes.
paper.athleteDev: Protect sleep during heavy training blocks and travel, since sleep loss is linked to altered hormones, inflammation and muscle damage markers in athletes. Sleep hygiene is the practical lever the review discusses.
paper.rtp: The review does not provide evidence that sleep extension speeds return to sport or lowers re-injury risk. It can support sleep as part of recovery planning, but it should not be used to set return-to-play timelines.

records.sourceFile: How much sleep does an elite athlete need.pdf

paper.citation: Sargent C, Lastella M, Halson SL, Roach GD. How Much Sleep Does an Elite Athlete Need? Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2021.
paper.abstract: Elite athletes' self-assessed sleep need was compared with an objective measure of habitual sleep duration in 175 athletes from 12 sports over about 12 nights of normal training. Athletes needed 8.3 hours of sleep to feel rested but averaged 6.7 hours, and only 3% obtained enough sleep to meet their stated need. Habitual sleep duration was shorter in individual than team sport athletes.
paper.tldr: Most elite athletes in this sample slept about 1.6 hours less than the sleep they said they needed to feel rested. Earlier sleep onset and later wake times were associated with longer sleep, and the authors suggest the data can serve as normative sleep targets.
paper.methods: Participants were 175 elite athletes (30 women) aged 22.2 (3.8) years from 12 sports, excluding those who were injured, at altitude, had a sleep disorder or had recent transmeridian travel. Sleep need was asked as a single question, and sleep was recorded over an average of 12 nights with sleep diaries and wrist activity monitors. A sleep deficit index was calculated as sleep need minus habitual sleep duration, and mixed models compared sports, sport types and sexes.
paper.findings: Athletes reported a sleep need of 8.3 (0.9) hours and habitual sleep of 6.7 (0.8) hours, a deficit of 96.0 (60.6) minutes, and only 3% met their need. Habitual sleep was shorter in individual than team sport athletes (d = 0.6), although sleep need did not differ (d = 0.2). Earlier sleep onset and later wake times were associated with longer sleep, and female athletes went to bed earlier than male athletes, with no sex difference in sleep duration.
paper.limitations: Sleep need came from a single question, and wrist monitors can over- or underestimate sleep by tens of minutes. Daytime naps were not recorded, so total sleep may be underestimated. Only 30 women were included, and sex comparisons were across sports rather than within sport. The text describes 12 sports, but Table 1 lists 14 (including one alpine skier and one diver).
paper.practicalImplications: Use the 8.3-hour self-reported sleep need as a reference, recognising that individual need ranged from 5.5 to 11 hours. Earlier sleep onset and later sleep offset were associated with longer sleep, so the authors suggest reviewing training start times (especially sessions before 6 AM) and allowing later wake times after evening sessions. Their suggested targets of sleep starting 22:00 to 22:30 or ending 09:00 to 09:30 come from these associations and were not tested as interventions.
paper.athleteDev: Use the athlete's self-reported sleep need and sleep logs to set practical sleep targets, and check whether training start times leave enough time for sleep. Individual sports athletes in this sample slept less than team sport athletes, so monitor them closely. Sleep schedule changes were not tested for performance benefit in this study.
paper.rtp: The study did not include injured athletes and does not address return to sport. It should not be used to set sleep requirements for rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: How to manage travel fatigue and jet lag in athletes - A systematic review of interventions.pdf

paper.citation: Janse van Rensburg DC, Jansen van Rensburg A, Fowler P, Fullagar H, Stevens D, Halson S, et al. How to manage travel fatigue and jet lag in athletes? A systematic review of interventions. Br J Sports Med. 2020.
paper.abstract: The authors systematically reviewed exercise, sleep, light, nutrition, and pharmacological interventions for travel fatigue and jet lag in athletes, using studies from athletes and, where none existed, healthy populations. They found no studies on travel fatigue and 12 athlete-specific jet lag studies, with the evidence graded as low quality for successful jet lag management in athletes.
paper.tldr: There is no research-based evidence on managing travel fatigue in athletes, and the athlete jet lag evidence is low quality. Judiciously timed exercise may help, and melatonin may be important, but both need larger athlete studies before they can be recommended.
paper.methods: Systematic review following PRISMA, registered on PROSPERO, searching PubMed, MEDLINE, CINAHL, Google Scholar and SPORTDiscus from inception to March 2019. Eligible studies were RCTs and non-randomised trials of interventions in travel-based or laboratory-based phase shifts, with athlete-specific studies preferred. Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane tool (RCTs) and Downs and Black (non-RCTs), and certainty was graded with GRADE. A meta-analysis was judged not feasible.
paper.findings: No studies on travel fatigue were found. For jet lag, 12 athlete-specific studies were found (6 non-randomised, 6 randomised). Exercise (4 studies) suggested that timing matters. Napping had some positive influence in two laboratory studies and a breathing and sleep CD intervention had no benefit, but the authors concluded the evidence does not support sleep interventions. Light gave contrasting results: an uncontrolled multifactorial study reported faster resynchronisation, while an RCT in 22 elite female soccer players found no clear benefit. That multifactorial study (melatonin, light and exercise) reported 2.13 days to resynchronise against an expected 6 days. Athlete-specific evidence was graded very low to low; stimulant and melatonin analogue findings (graded moderate) and nutrition findings (very low) came only from healthy non-athlete studies.
paper.limitations: No meta-analysis was possible because of heterogeneity in populations, flight direction, protocols, outcomes and circadian phase measurement. Athlete-specific studies had small samples, and many had no control group. The melatonin and light studies were multifactorial, so the effect of each component cannot be separated. The search was expanded to healthy populations for some interventions. The abstract describes the athlete evidence as low quality, while most athlete-specific GRADE ratings in the tables are very low (the sleep RCTs and the light RCT were rated low).
paper.practicalImplications: Do not treat any travel fatigue intervention as evidence-based for athletes yet. If a team tries judiciously timed exercise for jet lag (the authors suggest outdoor sessions, since appropriate exercise and light timing appear to coincide), it should record outcomes carefully, since the athlete evidence is low to very low quality. The authors are hesitant to recommend sedatives for regular jet lag management and do not recommend first-generation antihistamines or glucocorticoids. Melatonin use is restricted in some countries, and athletes must follow WADA rules.
paper.athleteDev: Use the review as a map of what has and has not been tested, not as a protocol. Judiciously timed exercise is the most-studied athlete option for jet lag (four small studies), while light gave contrasting results, and all of this evidence is low to very low quality. Any intervention used in athletes should be checked against current WADA rules before use.
paper.rtp: The review does not address return to sport or rehabilitation. Its findings relate to travel fatigue and jet lag in athletes who are competing and should not be used for injury return decisions.

records.sourceFile: Impact of evening blue light exposure timing on sleep, motor, and cognitive performance in young athletes with intermediate chronotype.pdf

paper.citation: Souissi MA, Gouasmia C, Dergaa I, Faleh J, Trabelsi O, Weiss K, et al. Impact of evening blue light exposure timing on sleep, motor, and cognitive performance in young athletes with intermediate chronotype. Biology of Sport. 2025;42(3):61-68.
paper.abstract: Randomized crossover study of 16 healthy male adolescent athletes with intermediate chronotype, exposed to a tablet video in four evening conditions: no exposure, 19:30 to 21:00, 21:00 to 22:30, and 22:30 to 00:00. Later exposure reduced total sleep time, lengthened sleep onset, and worsened dart-throwing accuracy, movement duration and selective attention. The authors conclude that evening blue light, especially after 21:00, harms sleep, motor and cognitive performance in young athletes.
paper.tldr: Watching a tablet in the late evening, especially after 9 PM, shortened self-reported sleep and worsened next-morning dart accuracy and attention in 16 adolescent male athletes. The study is small and tested single nights, so it does not show longer-term or training effects.
paper.methods: Randomized crossover design with four conditions in random order and 72-hour washouts. Participants watched the same neutral video on an 11-inch tablet during each exposure window, with a fixed bedtime of 00:00 and wake-up at 08:30. Outcomes were the Spiegel and Vis-Morgen questionnaires, dart-throwing accuracy and movement duration (video-analysed), and the Bells Test; analysis used one-way repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc tests.
paper.findings: Total sleep time was lower after exposure from 21:00 to 22:30 (442 minutes) and from 22:30 to 00:00 (428.5 minutes) than in control (465.5 minutes), and sleep latency was longest after the latest window (31.4 vs 20.1 minutes). Dart-throwing accuracy and selective attention were lower after the two later exposures, and movement duration was longer, with partial eta squared of 0.47 to 0.51 for accuracy and movement duration. Subjective sleep freshness did not differ between conditions.
paper.limitations: The authors acknowledge the small sample, the brief exposure, and that training schedules and diet were not controlled. Sleep outcomes were questionnaire-based with no objective sleep measure, and bedtime was fixed at midnight right after the latest exposure. The paper reports F(2,26) for selective attention where F(3,45) would be expected, contains a leftover generated sentence in the reference list ('Here are the remaining references (21-45)...'), and cites references by numbers that do not match the list (for example Phillips et al. [39] is absent and [39] is the Bells Test paper).
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches and athletes could limit tablet and phone use after about 21:00 before next-morning skill sessions, because exposure in the 21:00 to 00:00 windows reduced self-reported sleep and next-morning performance in this sample, while 19:30 to 21:00 exposure did not differ from control. The authors also suggest blue-light filters or blue-light-blocking glasses, but the study did not test those interventions.
paper.athleteDev: Late-evening tablet use was linked with less sleep and worse next-morning dart accuracy and attention in this small sample of adolescent athletes. A screen curfew before about 21:00 is a low-cost sleep habit to try, but the study does not show that it improves sport-specific skill beyond this task.
paper.rtp: The study used healthy adolescents with no injuries, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. Its sleep findings may matter for recovery, but they do not test injured athletes or return to play.

records.sourceFile: Impact of long-haul airline travel on athletic performance and recovery - A critical review of the literature.pdf

paper.citation: Botonis PG, Toubekis AG, Hill DW, Mündel T. Impact of long-haul airline travel on athletic performance and recovery: A critical review of the literature. Experimental Physiology. 2025;1-19.
paper.abstract: This narrative review summarizes studies of athletes and physically active participants who travelled west or east across four or more time zones. The authors cover aerobic, anaerobic, strength and power, perceptual, sleep and jet lag outcomes, and discuss travel, testing, timing, team, trait and tournament factors. They conclude that anaerobic and strength measures are negatively affected, endurance evidence is equivocal, and no particular recovery time can be established.
paper.tldr: After long-haul travel across four or more time zones, anaerobic power, muscle power and strength can be reduced for several days, and eastbound travel is generally more disruptive. The authors state that no single recovery time applies to every athlete.
paper.methods: Narrative review with no described systematic search. The authors limited the evidence to athletes or physically active participants travelling west or east across four or more time zones. They organized the findings by aerobic power, anaerobic power and capacity, strength and power, perceptual and psychophysiological variables, and sleep and jet lag, and summarized the included studies in a table.
paper.findings: Anaerobic power, muscle power and strength were reduced after transmeridian travel in several studies, with deterioration estimated at up to about 3 days after westbound and 4 days after eastbound travel. Endurance results were inconsistent, and sleep was disrupted after eastbound travel across seven or eight time zones. Eastbound travel produced more severe and longer jet lag symptoms, and one study reported jet lag persisting for up to 13 days after a seven-zone trip.
paper.limitations: No search strategy, databases or inclusion process are described, so study selection cannot be checked. The authors note that sex differences and chronotype were rarely examined, that sprint and jump tests may not reflect all sport demands, and that only one study measured anaerobic capacity after travel, and it is over 30 years old. The authors' views on teams, traits and tournaments are presented as perspectives rather than tested findings.
paper.practicalImplications: Plan for performance and sleep disruption to last several days after long-haul travel rather than assuming it resolves on arrival. The authors estimate that anaerobic and strength decrements may last up to about 3 days after westbound and 4 days after eastbound travel, and conclude that recovery may need more than 3 days, with eastbound travel generally more disruptive. Protect sleep after arrival, since sleep loss was linked to larger performance and jet lag effects, and test at a matched time of day because testing time can confound results.
paper.athleteDev: Expect anaerobic power, muscle power and strength to be reduced for several days after long-haul travel, with eastbound travel generally more disruptive. Use sprint and jump tests at a matched time of day when monitoring readiness after travel. Do not assume endurance performance is affected, since the evidence is inconsistent, and do not use the 0.5 or 1 day per time zone rule as a fixed timeline.
paper.rtp: This review does not address injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions, and it cannot set clearance criteria. Its findings describe performance changes in healthy athletes after travel, not after injury.

records.sourceFile: Impact-Induced Muscle Damage and Contact Sports- Etiology, Effects on Neuromuscular Function and Recovery, and the Modulating Effects of Adaptation and Recovery Strategies.pdf

paper.citation: Naughton M, Miller J, Slater GJ. Impact-Induced Muscle Damage and Contact Sports: Etiology, Effects on Neuromuscular Function and Recovery, and the Modulating Effects of Adaptation and Recovery Strategies. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2018.
paper.abstract: This brief review compares impact-induced muscle damage (IIMD) from collisions in contact sports with exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD). The authors summarize the etiology of both, their effects on neuromuscular function and recovery, the repeated-bout effect, and recovery strategies. They conclude that IIMD appears distinct from EIMD, that its time course is not established, and that recovery evidence is largely drawn from EIMD and animal studies.
paper.tldr: Collisions in contact sports can cause muscle damage that differs from eccentric exercise damage. Controlled studies with simulated collisions show reduced power and sprint performance, but the time course of this damage and the best recovery strategies are not established.
paper.methods: Narrative review with no described systematic search. The authors reviewed human contact-sport studies, animal contusion and drop-mass models, and EIMD research, and used EIMD recovery studies to inform strategies where IIMD data were lacking.
paper.findings: Controlled simulated-collision studies in contact-sport athletes found decrements in power and mean sprint time after IIMD compared with nonimpact control conditions, while blood marker and soreness responses were inconsistent. In a rugby match study, the number of tackles was strongly associated with peak myoglobin (r = .852) and peak creatine kinase (r = .922). Animal drop-mass models reported reductions in isometric force, power and submaximal work at 1 hour (28% to 33%) and 48 hours (28% to 38%), and the authors judge the evidence on adaptation to IIMD equivocal.
paper.limitations: Most controlled human IIMD studies included wrestling, high-intensity running or other exercise that may have produced EIMD, which the authors note may confound results. Recovery strategies for IIMD are supported only by animal contusion models, and the authors state that anti-inflammatory approaches need caution because inflammation is needed for regeneration. The text describes no search strategy.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not assume that EIMD recovery timelines apply to collision exposure, since the authors state the IIMD time course is undefined. After collision-heavy sessions, monitor power, sprint and soreness responses over several days, because controlled studies show decrements in these measures. Use caution with anti-inflammatory recovery strategies after contact, because the review notes that inflammation supports regeneration.
paper.athleteDev: Expect power and sprint performance to decline after simulated collision work, and track these measures after collision-heavy training. Do not assume that EIMD recovery timelines describe collision exposure, since the time course of IIMD is not established. Strategies with EIMD support, such as cold-water immersion and tart cherry juice, have not been tested against collision damage in athletes.
paper.rtp: This review cannot define when a contact athlete is ready to return to play after collision-induced muscle damage, because the IIMD recovery timeline is undefined and controlled human data are limited. It does not provide return-to-sport criteria, and its animal and EIMD evidence cannot be used to set clearance timing.

records.sourceFile: Improving sleep quality to enhance athletic activity - The role of nutrition and supplementation - A mini-short review.pdf

paper.citation: Fusi J, Scarfò G, Di Silvestro R, Franzoni F. Improving Sleep Quality to Enhance Athletic Activity, the Role of Nutrition and Supplementation: A Mini-Short Review. Nutrients. 2025;17:1779.
paper.abstract: This mini-short narrative review summarizes how sleep loss affects athletes and how nutrition, supplements and exercise may influence sleep. It covers caffeine, magnesium, melatonin, tryptophan, ashwagandha and apigenin, and it concludes that the evidence in athletes is conflicting and needs more study.
paper.tldr: Sleep loss can impair athletic recovery and some kinds of performance, but this short review finds the evidence for specific supplements and exercise strategies for sleep in athletes limited and conflicting. Its firmest points are that evening caffeine disrupts sleep and that a low-glycemic, tryptophan-rich diet is the authors' preferred dietary approach.
paper.methods: Narrative review with no described search strategy, inclusion criteria or appraisal method. The authors summarize sleep physiology, sleep loss and performance, dietary carbohydrate and macronutrients, and six supplements, drawing mainly on individual trials and meta-analyses.
paper.findings: The review reports that sleep loss can reduce endurance and some skill performance and can slow recovery. It cites evidence that evening caffeine reduces sleep quantity and quality, and that high-glycemic meals have different effects in sedentary people and in athletes after training. It reports that melatonin, tryptophan (at 1 g or more), magnesium and ashwagandha improved some sleep outcomes in some non-athlete trials, while magnesium supplement users did not differ in sleep duration in one large survey. The authors conclude that a Mediterranean diet with low-glycemic and tryptophan-rich foods seems best for sleep, and that regular exercise can improve sleep.
paper.limitations: The review has no described search method, so the evidence base cannot be reproduced. It relies heavily on non-athlete populations, and several supplement claims rest on single small trials or on animal and mechanistic work. The authors acknowledge that the findings on nutrition, supplements and sport are conflicting.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can use the review to support advising athletes to avoid caffeine in the evening before sleep. Staff should not treat the supplement doses in the review as validated sport protocols, since they come mainly from non-athlete trials. The authors suggest, without testing it, that a final taper session with sleep-promoting exercises could be included in a training program.
paper.athleteDev: The review links sleep loss to slower recovery, higher perceived exertion and, in some tasks, lower performance, which supports prioritizing sleep in athlete programs. It does not provide a validated supplement or meal plan to improve performance through sleep.
paper.rtp: The review does not address injury rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions. It may inform general recovery advice, but it should not be used to set sleep or nutrition criteria for clearance after injury.

records.sourceFile: Inadequate sleep and muscle                        strength- Implications for resistance training - Copy.pdf

paper.citation: Knowles OE, Drinkwater EJ, Urwin CS, Lamon S, Aisbett B. Inadequate sleep and muscle strength: Implications for resistance training. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2018; article in press.
paper.abstract: This systematic review of 17 studies examined the effects of sleep deprivation and sleep restriction on resistance exercise performance and on hormonal markers of muscle protein metabolism. One night of deprivation had little effect on strength, consecutive nights of restriction reduced multi-joint force output, and hormonal results conflicted.
paper.tldr: Losing one night of sleep did little to maximal strength in most of the studies reviewed, while the one study of three nights of 3 h sleep found lower 1RM in multi-joint lifts. Caffeine, group training and training before long waking periods are suggested to protect performance, but each rests on very few studies.
paper.methods: Systematic search of five electronic databases for English-language studies of sleep deprivation or restriction with resistance exercise performance or hormonal outcomes, following PRISMA. Two reviewers screened, extracted data and rated quality with the EPHPP tool. Seventeen studies were included, covering athletes, military personnel and other adults; no shiftwork studies met the criteria.
paper.findings: Seven studies examined one night of restriction and one examined three consecutive nights. In the multi-night study (8 trained men, 3 h sleep), 1RM fell for leg press, deadlift and bench press but not biceps curl. After one night of restriction, total resistance-training workload fell in professional rugby players and strength fell only with afternoon testing after early waking in judo athletes, while other studies found no change. One night of total deprivation had little or no effect on maximal strength in most studies, and cortisol and testosterone findings were inconsistent.
paper.limitations: The authors rated 13 studies as moderate and 4 as weak quality, and none reached strong quality because blinding of participants is not possible. Only one study tested consecutive nights of restriction and only two used a resistance training session, athlete studies were few and mostly used severe sleep loss, and only four studies included women. The abstract states that inadequate sleep impairs compound-movement strength, which is firmer than the evidence base the authors themselves describe as limited.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff who schedule heavy compound lifts after several very short nights may plan for lower force output, though this rests on one small study. Caffeine, group sessions and training before long waking periods are suggested as ways to protect performance, but they rest on very few studies and should be tested in the athletes staff work with.
paper.athleteDev: Multi-joint strength may fall after several nights of very short sleep, but a single night of sleep loss had little effect on maximal strength in most studies. The review suggests that caffeine, group training or training before long waking periods may help, but these were tested in very few studies.
paper.rtp: The review does not study injured athletes or rehabilitation. It cannot set return-to-play strength criteria, although it may inform how sleep loss is considered when interpreting strength tests during rehabilitation or return.

records.sourceFile: Intraindividual variability in sleep among athletes  - A systematic review of definitions, operationalizations, and key correlates.pdf

paper.citation: Kemp S, Spence AL, Keller BS, Ducker KJ, Gucciardi DF. Intraindividual variability in sleep among athletes: A systematic review of definitions, operationalizations, and key correlates. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2023.
paper.abstract: This systematic review with narrative synthesis examined how researchers have defined, measured and studied intraindividual variability in athlete sleep across 16 eligible studies. Few studies defined the concept, and most measured variability as deviation from each athlete's typical sleep, usually with standard deviation or coefficient of variation. The authors rate the overall quality of the evidence as moderate and propose a working definition of sleep variability to guide future research.
paper.tldr: Research on athlete sleep variability rarely defines the concept, and the methods used to measure it vary widely. Anyone tracking night-to-night sleep variability should state how it was calculated, because the result depends on the measure chosen.
paper.methods: This preregistered review followed PRISMA 2020 and searched six databases from inception to April 2022, plus reference lists and citations. Two authors screened titles and abstracts together using a machine-learning ranking tool; eligible studies sampled athletes and recorded sleep daily for at least three nights by self-report or wearable device, and polysomnography-only studies were excluded. Data were extracted by one author, with a random 30% checked by a second, and study quality was rated on a bespoke eight-item tool.
paper.findings: From 1,209 records, 16 observational studies met the criteria, published between 2015 and 2022 and sampling 937 athletes. Only four studies gave an explicit definition of sleep variability, and all but one study measured variability as deviation from a typical level, most often with intraindividual standard deviation (n = 8) or coefficient of variation (n = 6). Sample size justification was absent in all studies, and missing data were not reported in 62.5%. The authors propose a working definition: the magnitude of temporally heterogeneous deviations, for each 24-hour sleep cycle, from one's typical level of sleep indicators across a finite period.
paper.limitations: The search did not seek unpublished work such as preprints, was limited to English, and quality was rated with a bespoke tool. The synthesis is narrative, the included studies are small and observational, and the authors describe knowledge of determinants and outcomes of sleep variability as in its infancy, so the proposed definition is not yet tested. The authors also note that standard deviation and coefficient of variation indices have known weaknesses (poor reliability, correlation with the mean), and found no consensus on the minimum number of nights needed.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff who monitor athlete sleep may consider night-to-night variability alongside average sleep duration, because the authors argue that averages alone can hide meaningful differences between athletes. The review does not provide thresholds for harmful variability, so variability should be treated as an additional indicator to watch, not a validated cut-off. Any internal report should state the measure used (standard deviation, coefficient of variation or z score), the number of nights and how missing data were handled.
paper.athleteDev: The review supports tracking how far an athlete's sleep moves from their own typical pattern, as well as average sleep, when planning training and performance. It did not synthesise links between sleep variability and performance, so its value for training decisions is not yet established.
paper.rtp: The review does not examine injury, recovery or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions. It cannot say whether a given level of sleep variability is safe for an athlete to return at.

records.sourceFile: Investigating the sleep habits in individual and team-sport athletes using the Athlete Sleep Behavior Questionnaire and the Pittsburgh Sleep Qua.pdf

paper.citation: Driller MW, Suppiah H, Rogerson D, Ruddock A, James L, Virgile A. Investigating the sleep habits in individual and team-sport athletes using the Athlete Sleep Behavior Questionnaire and the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. Sleep Sci 2022;15(1):112-117.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional survey compared sleep behaviours and self-reported sleep in 137 individual-sport and 270 team-sport elite adult athletes using the ASBQ and PSQI. Individual-sport athletes reported slightly longer sleep and higher sleep efficiency, while PSQI global scores did not differ. Team-sport athletes scored worse on the ASBQ global score and on several items, including stimulant use, alcohol before bed and travel disrupting routines.
paper.tldr: Team-sport athletes in this sample reported more maladaptive pre-sleep behaviours than individual-sport athletes, and slightly shorter, less efficient sleep. The differences are small and self-reported, so they point to behaviours worth addressing rather than a reliable group-level sleep problem.
paper.methods: A convenience sample of 407 elite athletes from 16 sports and nine countries, who were at least four weeks into the in-season phase, completed the ASBQ (18 items) and PSQI (19 items) online for the past four weeks. Independent t tests compared individual-sport and team-sport athletes for each questionnaire and item, with Cohen's d for effect sizes. Athletes were classed as individual-sport (n = 137) or team-sport (n = 270).
paper.findings: Individual-sport athletes reported longer total sleep time (7:57 vs 7:40 h:mm, p = 0.04, d = 0.28) and higher sleep efficiency (91.1% vs 88.6%, p = 0.009, d = 0.29). PSQI global scores did not differ (team 5.4, individual 5.2, p = 0.51). The ASBQ global score was higher in team-sport athletes (44.3 vs 42.6, p = 0.004, d = 0.30), who also reported more stimulant use with training or competition (p = 0.0001), alcohol within 4 hours of bed (p = 0.005) and travel disrupting their routine (p = 0.03). Team-sport athletes also reported more night waking and feeling too hot.
paper.limitations: This is a self-reported, cross-sectional convenience sample across nine countries, with the team-sport group dominated by rugby union. The effect sizes are small, the design cannot show causes, and no correction for multiple comparisons is described. The authors note that the sports differ in training time and style, so the team and individual split may hide differences between endurance and strength or power sports.
paper.practicalImplications: Practitioners working with team-sport squads could review stimulant use, alcohol timing and travel schedules, since these were the items where team-sport athletes scored worst. Pre-sleep screen use, going to bed sore and worrying in bed were common across the whole cohort and are reasonable targets for education. Because the group differences are small and self-reported, individual sleep assessment should guide any specific plan rather than assuming a whole squad needs the same intervention.
paper.athleteDev: Staff could use the ASBQ items where team-sport athletes scored worst, such as stimulant use, late alcohol and travel disruption, to plan targeted sleep education in training camps and competition schedules. The study did not measure performance outcomes, so any performance benefit is not shown.
paper.rtp: The study is not about injury or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions. Sleep behaviours such as worry in bed or late stimulant use may be relevant to recovery after injury, but no recovery or injury outcomes were measured.

records.sourceFile: Irregular sleep-wake patterns in student-athletes exposed to early morning training.pdf

paper.citation: Wilson SMB, Jones MI, Draper SB, Parker JK. Irregular sleep/wake patterns in student-athletes exposed to early morning training. J Sports Sci 2025.
paper.abstract: This observational study measured sleep and sleep regularity in 21 male student rugby union players over two weeks using wrist actigraphy. Nights before morning training were shorter and started and ended earlier than nights before free mornings, and the Sleep Regularity Index was low overall. The authors conclude that early morning training contributes to irregular sleep in student-athletes and should be scheduled at another time where feasible.
paper.tldr: Student-athletes who start training at 06:30 to 07:00 slept about 1.8 hours less the night before and had irregular sleep timing across the week. The authors recommend later training where feasible, but this single-team study cannot show that a later start would improve sleep.
paper.methods: Twenty-eight male players from one university rugby union team were recruited, and 21 with at least five days of valid actigraphy were analysed. Sleep was measured for two weeks in October 2023 with GENEActiv wrist monitors and a sleep diary that recorded naps and training attendance. The Sleep Regularity Index (SRI) was calculated, and nights before morning training were compared with free mornings using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, with Friedman tests and Bonferroni post-hoc tests across days, and with correlations against SRI. Players also completed the Athlete Sleep Screening Questionnaire for sleep screening and chronotype.
paper.findings: Nights before morning training (n = 109) had a shorter median total sleep time (5.86 vs 7.66 h, r = 0.67), a shorter sleep period, and earlier sleep onset (23:07 vs 00:00, about 0.9 h earlier) and offset (05:45 vs 08:57, about 3.2 h earlier) than nights before free mornings (n = 121); 85.3% of nights before training had under 7 h of sleep, against 33.8% before free mornings. The median SRI was 67.0 (IQR 17.0), and 9 of 21 players (42.9%) had an SRI in the lowest 10th percentile of UK Biobank data (below 65.1). Lower SRI was associated with more cumulative sleep including naps (r = -0.62), later sleep onset (r = -0.50) and offset (r = -0.60) and a later chronotype (r = 0.52), but not with nocturnal sleep time, and nappers had lower SRI than non-nappers (57.9 vs 73.6, p = 0.004).
paper.limitations: The sample is 21 male players from one team over two weeks, so the findings may not apply to women, other sports or a full season. Sleep was measured by wrist actigraphy and diaries, and the actigraphy device cited has a specificity of 45% against polysomnography. The authors did not control academic timetables or off-campus travel, which may have affected sleep, and the design cannot show that early training causes the irregularity.
paper.practicalImplications: Where feasible, coaches and performance staff could move morning sessions later, as the authors recommend, because nights before morning training were much shorter and most fell under 7 hours. Staff could monitor sleep regularity as well as duration, since sleep timing shifted by up to about 3 hours between training and free days. Any change to training times should be checked for its effect on sleep, because the study did not test whether a later start improves sleep.
paper.athleteDev: Early training starts were associated with about 1.8 hours less sleep the night before, which may affect recovery and training quality, so training schedules are a practical lever for performance staff. The study did not measure performance, and the authors say the link between sleep regularity and sports performance is unclear.
paper.rtp: The study did not examine injury or return to sport, and players with a concussion since the start of the season were excluded, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions. Its findings on sleep timing may be relevant to sleep planning during rehabilitation, but this was not tested.

records.sourceFile: Is reaction time altered by mental or physical exertion.pdf

paper.citation: Le Mansec Y, Dorel S, Nordez A, Jubeau M. Is reaction time altered by mental or physical exertion? European Journal of Applied Physiology. 2019;119:1323-1335.
paper.abstract: This study assessed the effects of mental effort and muscle effort on simple reaction time and its components, premotor time and electromechanical delay (EMD). Thirteen men completed a mental arithmetic task, an isometric biceps fatiguing protocol, and a control task. Reaction time and premotor time remained stable in all conditions, and EMD increased only after muscle effort, mainly due to the passive part of the series elastic component. The authors conclude that neither mental nor muscle effort has a negative effect on simple reaction time during voluntary contractions.
paper.tldr: Fourteen minutes of mental arithmetic or a short biceps fatiguing protocol did not slow simple reaction time in healthy active men. Muscle fatigue did lengthen the electromechanical delay and reduce force production, so the reaction time result should not be read as full explosive readiness.
paper.methods: Randomised crossover design with three sessions at least one week apart: mental effort (14 minutes of serial subtraction), muscle effort (intermittent elbow flexor contractions to task failure) and a control movie. Simple visual reaction time was split into EMG-based premotor time and voluntary EMD, and EMD was also measured with electrical stimulation using ultrafast ultrasound. Maximal voluntary torque, voluntary activation, contractile properties, rate of force development and NASA-TLX scores were measured before and after each session and analysed with repeated-measures ANOVA.
paper.findings: Reaction time and premotor time did not change in any condition (all P > 0.05). After muscle effort, EMD rose during electrically evoked contractions (10.5 to 12.3 ms, P = 0.001), mainly due to an increase in the passive part of the series elastic component, and voluntary EMD rose by 25.6% without statistical significance. Maximal voluntary torque fell by 17.7% after muscle effort, and rate of force development over 50 to 100 ms fell by 31% to 42%.
paper.limitations: The study had 13 men, and the authors acknowledge that it may have been too small to detect small changes, creating a risk of a type 2 error. Reaction time was measured with only two or three trials to limit recovery, which reduces reliability, and only the biceps was recorded, so other elbow flexors could have driven the response.
paper.practicalImplications: A short mental task or a brief elbow flexor fatigue protocol did not slow simple reaction time in healthy active men, so an unchanged reaction time should not be taken as proof that a person is unaffected by fatigue. After heavy muscle work, staff should check explosive force capacity, because rate of force development fell substantially even though reaction time did not change.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, the study suggests that a simple reaction time test after fatiguing work may look normal even when force production is reduced. Rate of force development should be checked alongside reaction time when explosive actions matter.
paper.rtp: The study used healthy, active men after short, non-injurious protocols, and it does not assess injured athletes or any return-to-sport criteria, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.
